{{Short description|Annual high school maths competition}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2022}}

[[File:IMO logo.svg|thumb|Logo of the International Mathematical Olympiad]]

The '''International Mathematical Olympiad''' ('''IMO''') is an annual [[mathematical olympiad|mathematical competition]] for [[Student competition|pre-university students]], and is the oldest of the [[International Science Olympiad]]s.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://olympiads.win.tue.nl/imo/|title=International Mathematics Olympiad (IMO)|date=2008-02-01}}</ref> It is widely regarded as the most prestigious mathematical competition in the world.<ref>{{cite book
 | last = Kenderov | first = Petar S.
 | contribution = Competitions and mathematics education
 | isbn = 978-3-03719-022-7
 | mr = 2275743
 | pages = 1583–1598
 | quote = Of course, the most important and most prestigious math competition is the International Mathematical Olympiad
 | publisher = Eur. Math. Soc., Zürich
 | title = International Congress of Mathematicians. Vol. III
 | year = 2006}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = Saul | first1 = Mark
 | last2 = Vaderlind | first2 = Paul
 | id = {{EBSCOhost|156065775|dbcode=ehh}}
 | issue = 2
 | journal = Mathematics Competitions
 | pages = 9–19
 | title = The International Mathematical Olympiad, Age 62: What we Know and What we would Like to Know
 | volume = 34
 | year = 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite book
 | last1 = Veilande | first1 = Ingrida
 | last2 = Ramana | first2 = Liga
 | last3 = Krauze | first3 = Sandra
 | editor-last = Singer | editor-first = Florence Mihaela
 | title = Mathematical Creativity and Mathematical Giftedness: Enhancing Creative Capacities in Mathematically Promising Students
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-319-73156-8_13
 | isbn = 9783319731568
 | series = ICME-13 Monographs
 | pages = 343–372
 | publisher = Springer International Publishing
 | contribution = Repeated Participation at the Mathematical Olympiads: A Comparative Study of the Solutions of Selected Problems
 | year = 2018}}</ref> The first IMO was held in [[Socialist Republic of Romania|Romania]] in 1959. It has since been held annually, except in 1980. More than 100 countries participate. Each country sends a team of up to six students,<ref name = "more"/> plus one team leader, one deputy leader, and observers.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.akamai.com/html/about/press/releases/2001/press_070401.html|title=The International Mathematical Olympiad 2001 Presented by the Akamai Foundation Opens Today in Washington, D.C.|access-date=2008-03-05}}</ref>

The contest takes place over two days, and consists of six problems (three given on each day). The problems are extremely difficult, and may include topics not conventionally covered in school, but they avoid the use of [[calculus]]. Awards are given to approximately the top-scoring 50% of the individual contestants. Teams are not officially recognized—all scores are given only to individual contestants, but team scoring is unofficially compared more than individual scores.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imo-register.org.uk/1992-report.html|title=33rd International Mathematical Olympiad|access-date=2008-03-05|date=1992-07-21|author=Tony Gardiner|publisher=University of Birmingham}}</ref>

==Scoring and format==
The competition consists of six [[Mathematical problem|problems]]. The competition is held over two consecutive days with three problems each; each day, the contestants have four-and-a-half hours to solve three problems. Each problem is worth 7 points for a maximum total score of 42 points. [[Calculators]] are banned. [[Protractor]]s were banned relatively recently.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.edb.gov.hk/attachment/tc/curriculum-development/kla/ma/IMO/Nov20155-4online.pdf|title=IMO 2015 Report Leader's Perspective (I)|author= Law, Ka-Ho|magazine= IMOment: IMO 2016 Newsletter|issue= 5|year= 2015|page= 4}}</ref>

Each country's marks are agreed between that country's leader and deputy leader, and coordinators provided by the host country (the leader of the team whose country submitted the problem in the case of the marks of the host country), subject to the decisions of the chief coordinator and, ultimately, a jury if any disputes cannot be resolved.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://imo.wolfram.com/facts.html|title=IMO Facts from Wolfram|access-date=2008-03-05|archive-date=29 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120229122231/http://imo.wolfram.com/facts.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Question type===
Unlike other science olympiads, the IMO has no official syllabus and does not cover any university-level topics. The problems chosen are from various areas of secondary school mathematics, broadly classifiable as [[geometry]], [[number theory]], [[algebra]], and [[combinatorics]]. They require no knowledge of [[higher mathematics]] such as [[calculus]] and [[mathematical analysis|analysis]], and solutions are often elementary. However, they are usually disguised so as to make the solutions difficult. The problems given in the IMO are largely designed to require creativity and the ability to solve problems quickly. Thus, the prominently featured problems are algebraic [[inequality (mathematics)|inequalities]], [[complex numbers]], and [[compass and straightedge constructions|construction]]-oriented geometrical problems, though in recent years, the latter has not been as popular as before because of the algorithmic use of theorems like [[Muirhead's inequality]], and complex/analytic bashing to solve problems.<ref name=olson/>

The content ranges from extremely difficult [[algebra]] and pre-calculus problems to problems in branches of mathematics not conventionally covered in secondary or high school and often not at university level either, such as [[Projective geometry|projective]] and [[complex geometry]], [[functional equations]], [[combinatorics]], and well-grounded [[number theory]], of which extensive knowledge of theorems is required. Calculus, though allowed in solutions, is never required, as there is a principle that anyone with a basic understanding of mathematics should understand the problems, even if the solutions require a great deal more knowledge. Supporters of this principle claim that it allows more universality and creates an incentive to find elegant, deceptively simple-looking problems that nevertheless require a certain level of ingenuity, oftentimes a great deal of ingenuity, to net all points for a given IMO problem.<ref>{{cite book
 | title = Mathematical Olympiad Treasures
 | first1 = Titu | last1 = Andreescu
 | first2 = Bogdan | last2 = Enescu
 | year = 2012
 | edition = 2nd
 | page = v
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=550P8T4-1BAC&pg=PR5
 | publisher = Springer
| isbn = 978-0-8176-8253-8 }}</ref>

===Problem selection===
Each participating country, other than the host country, may submit suggested problems to a problem selection committee provided by the host country, which reduces the submitted problems to a shortlist. The team leaders arrive at the IMO a few days in advance of the contestants and form the IMO jury, which is responsible for all the formal decisions relating to the contest, starting with selecting the six problems from the shortlist. The jury aims to order the problems so that the order in increasing difficulty is Q1, Q4, Q2, Q5, Q3, and Q6, where the first day problems Q1, Q2, and Q3 are in increasing difficulty, and the second day problems Q4, Q5, and Q6 are in increasing difficulty. The team leaders of all countries are given the problems in advance of the contestants, and thus, are kept strictly separated and observed.<ref>{{Cite book
 |last=Djukić
 |first=Dušan
 |title=The IMO Compendium: A Collection of Problems Suggested for the International Olympiads, 1959–2004
 |publisher=Springer
 |year=2006
 |isbn=978-0-387-24299-6
 }}</ref>

==Team selection==
{{Main|International Mathematical Olympiad selection process}}
The selection process differs by country, but it often consists of a series of tests that admit fewer students at each test. Contestants must be under the age of 20 and must not be registered at any [[tertiary institution]]. Subject to these conditions, an individual may participate any number of times in the IMO.<ref name="otago">{{cite web|url=http://www.maths.otago.ac.nz/home/schools/gifted_children/olympiad.pdf|title=The International Mathematical Olympiad|access-date=2008-03-05|publisher=AMC|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080216122623/http://www.maths.otago.ac.nz/home/schools/gifted_children/olympiad.pdf|archive-date=2008-02-16|url-status=dead}}</ref>

[[File:Geo prob diagram.svg|thumb|200px|A stage in the process of solving a problem from the [[American Invitational Mathematics Examination|AIME]], part of the United States' selection process]]
In some countries, especially those in [[East Asia]], the selection process involves several tests of a difficulty comparable to the IMO itself.<ref>{{Cite book
 |last=Liu
 |first=Andy
 |author-link=Andy Liu (mathematician)
 |title=Chinese Mathematics Competitions and Olympiads
 |publisher=AMT Publishing
 |year=1998
 |isbn=1-876420-00-6
 }}</ref> The Chinese contestants go through a camp.<ref>Chen, Wang. Personal interview. February 19, 2008.</ref> In others, such as the United States, possible participants go through a series of easier standalone competitions that gradually increase in difficulty. In the United States, the tests include the [[American Mathematics Competitions]], the [[American Invitational Mathematics Examination]], and the [[United States of America Junior Mathematical Olympiad]]/[[United States of America Mathematical Olympiad]], each of which is a competition in its own right. For high scorers in the final competition for the team selection, there also is a [[Mathematical Olympiad Summer Program|summer camp]], like that of China.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.unl.edu/amc/|title=The American Mathematics Competitions|access-date=2008-03-05|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080302084024/http://www.unl.edu/amc/|archive-date=2008-03-02}}</ref>

In countries of the former [[Soviet Union]] and other eastern European countries, a team has in the past been chosen several years beforehand, and they are given special training specifically for the event. However, such methods have been discontinued in some countries.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.austms.org.au/Gazette/1997/Nov97/hunt.html|title=IMO 1997|access-date=2008-03-05|author=David C. Hunt|publisher=Australian Mathematical Society|archive-date=16 September 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090916040353/http://www.austms.org.au/Gazette/1997/Nov97/hunt.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

[[India]] selects its team for the IMO through a multi-stage selection process organized by the [[Homi Bhabha Centre for Science Education]] (HBCSE), a centre of the [[Tata Institute of Fundamental Research]] (TIFR). The selection process begins with the Indian Olympiad Qualifier in Mathematics (IOQM). Successful candidates qualify for the Regional Mathematical Olympiad (RMO). Top performers from the RMO are then selected for the [[Indian National Mathematical Olympiad]] (INMO), a national-level examination consisting of proof-oriented problems. Students who perform well in the INMO are invited to the International Mathematical Olympiad Training Camp (IMOTC), held annually at HBCSE or [[Chennai Mathematical Institute]]. During the camp, participants receive training in advanced mathematics and take a series of selection tests. Based on their overall performance throughout the camp, six students are selected to represent India at the International Mathematical Olympiad. The team is accompanied by a leader and a deputy leader appointed by HBCSE.<ref>{{citeweb|url=https://olympiads.hbcse.tifr.res.in/about-olympiads/stages/mathematical-olympiad/|title=Stages of Mathematical Olympiad|access-date=2026-07-25|publisher=HBCSE-TIFR}}</ref>

==Awards==
The participants are ranked based on their individual scores. Medals are awarded to the highest ranked participants; slightly fewer than half of them receive a medal. The cutoffs (minimum scores required to receive a gold, silver, or bronze medal respectively) are then chosen so that the numbers of gold, silver and bronze medals awarded are approximately in the ratios 1:2:3. Participants who do not win a medal but who score 7 points on at least one problem receive an honorable mention.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://imo.wolfram.com/scores/howmedals.html|title=How Medals Are Determined|access-date=2008-03-05|archive-date=1 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180101152211/http://imo.wolfram.com/scores/howmedals.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Special prizes may be awarded for solutions of outstanding elegance or involving good generalisations of a problem. This last happened in 1995 ([[Nikolay Nikolov (mathematician)|Nikolay Nikolov, Bulgaria]]) and 2005 (Iurie Boreico), but was more frequent up to the early 1980s.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://olympiads.win.tue.nl/imo/imo95/imo95reg.html|title=IMO '95 regulations|access-date=2008-03-05}}</ref> The special prize in 2005 was awarded to Iurie Boreico, a student from Moldova, for his solution to Problem 3, a three-variable inequality.<ref>{{cite web|title=USA and International Mathematical Olympiads: 2006-2007 |url=https://web.williams.edu/Mathematics/sjmiller/public_html/greenchicken/otherexams/olympiad0607solns.pdf|editor-first1=Zuming|editor-last1=Feng|editor-first2=Yufei|editor-last2=Zhao}}</ref>

The rule that at most half the contestants win a medal is sometimes broken if it would cause the total number of medals to deviate too much from half the number of contestants. This last happened in 2010 (when the choice was to give either 226 (43.71%) or 266 (51.45%) of the 517 contestants (excluding the 6 from North Korea — see below) a medal),<ref name="award">{{cite web|url=http://official.imo2011.nl/year_individual_r.aspx?year=2010|title=51st International Mathematical Olympiad Results|access-date=2011-07-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629113735/http://official.imo2011.nl/year_individual_r.aspx?year=2010|archive-date=2011-06-29|url-status=dead}}</ref> 2012 (when the choice was to give either 226 (41.24%) or 277 (50.55%) of the 548 contestants a medal), and 2013, when the choice was to give either 249 (47.16%) or 278 (52.65%) of the 528 contestants a medal. In these cases, slightly more than half the contestants were awarded a medal.<ref name=imo2011>{{cite web |url=https://www.imo-official.org/year_individual_r.aspx?year=2011&column=total&order=desc |title=52nd IMO 2011 – Individual results|publisher=International Mathematical Olympiad |accessdate=2022-07-17}}</ref><ref name=imo2012>{{cite web |url=https://www.imo-official.org/year_individual_r.aspx?year=2012&column=total&order=desc |title=53rd IMO 2012 – Individual results|publisher=International Mathematical Olympiad |accessdate=2022-07-17}}</ref>

[[File:IMO_2015_closing_ceremony.jpg|thumb|200px|Some of gold medal contestants during the IMO 2015 closing ceremony, Chiang Mai Thailand]]

==History==
{{see also|List of International Mathematical Olympiads}}
The first IMO was held in Romania in 1959. Since then it has been held every year (except in 1980, when it was cancelled due to internal strife in Mongolia).<ref>{{cite journal |last=Turner |first=Nura D. |title=A Historical Sketch of Olympiads: U.S.A. and International |journal=The College Mathematics Journal |volume=16 |issue=5 |year=1985 |pages=330–335 |doi=10.1080/07468342.1985.11972906|jstor=2686992 }}</ref> It was initially founded for eastern European member countries of the [[Warsaw Pact]], under the [[USSR]] bloc of influence, but later other countries participated as well.<ref name = "more"/> Because of this eastern origin, the IMOs were first hosted only in eastern European countries, and gradually spread to other nations.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sms.math.nus.edu.sg/Simo/Simo.aspx|title=Singapore International Mathematical Olympiad (SIMO) Home Page|access-date=2008-02-04|publisher=Singapore Mathematical Society|archive-date=27 March 2003|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030327035236/http://sms.math.nus.edu.sg/Simo/Simo.aspx|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Sources differ about the cities hosting some of the early IMOs. This may be partly because leaders and students are generally housed at different locations, and partly because after the competition the students were sometimes based in multiple cities for the rest of the IMO. The exact dates cited may also differ, because of leaders arriving before the students, and at more recent IMOs the IMO Advisory Board arriving before the leaders.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://blog.medallia.com/2006/07/norwegian_students_in_internat.html|title=Norwegian Students in International Mathematical Olympiad|access-date=2008-03-05|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061020100605/http://blog.medallia.com/2006/07/norwegian_students_in_internat.html|archive-date=2006-10-20}}</ref>

Several students, such as [[Lisa Sauermann]], [[Peter Scholze]], [[Reid W. Barton]], [[Nicușor Dan]] (notably elected President of Romania in 2025) and [[Ciprian Manolescu]] have [[List of International Mathematical Olympiad participants#High-scoring participants|performed exceptionally well]] in the IMO, winning multiple gold medals. Others, such as [[Terence Tao]], [[Artur Avila]], [[Grigori Perelman]], [[Ngô Bảo Châu]], [[Peter Scholze]] and [[Maryam Mirzakhani]] have gone on to become notable [[mathematician]]s. Several former participants [[List of International Mathematical Olympiad participants#Notable participants|have won awards]] such as the [[Fields Medal]].<ref>{{cite journal
 |last=Lord
 |first=Mary
 |author-link=Mary Lord (correspondent)
 |title=Michael Jordans of math - U.S. Student whizzes stun the cipher world 
 |journal=[[U.S. News & World Report]]
 |volume=131 
 |issue=3 
 |page=26 
 |date=July 23, 2001
 |url=http://search.ebscohost.com/login.aspx?direct=true&db=a9h&AN=4818783&site=ehost-live
 }}</ref>

Shortly after the 2016 International Mathematical Olympiad in [[Hong Kong]], [[North Korea]]n child prodigy [[Ri Jong-yol]] made his way to the [[Consulate General of South Korea, Hong Kong|South Korean consulate general]], where he sought refuge for two months. Chinese authorities eventually allowed him to leave Hong Kong on a flight to [[Seoul]].<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Caesar |first=Ed |title=The Incredible Rise of North Korea's Hacking Army |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2021/04/26/the-incredible-rise-of-north-koreas-hacking-army |access-date=9 July 2024 |magazine=[[The New Yorker]] |date=19 April 2021 }}</ref>

The 61st IMO, scheduled to be held in [[St. Petersburg, Russia]] in 2020, was instead held virtually because of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], the first time this had occurred.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://maa.org/news/u-s-team-places-third-at-the-61st-international-mathematical-olympiad/|title=U.S. Team Places Third at the 61st International Mathematical Olympiad|publisher=Mathematical Association of America|date=October 20, 2020|access-date=2025-12-30}}</ref> The 62nd IMO in 2021 was also held virtually.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://maa.org/news/team-usa-earns-fourth-place-at-62nd-international-mathematical-olympiad/|title=Team USA Earns Fourth Place at 62nd International Mathematical Olympiad|publisher=Mathematical Association of America|date=August 3, 2021|access-date=2025-12-30}}</ref>

At the 2025 IMO, both [[OpenAI]] and [[Google DeepMind]] claimed that their systems could have achieved a gold-medal level performance in the competition.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Varanasi |first=Lakshmi |title=OpenAI just won gold at the world's most prestigious math competition. Here's why that's a big deal. |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/openai-gold-iom-math-competition-2025-7 |access-date=2026-08-24 |website=Business Insider |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Lockhart |first=Thang Luong and Edward |date=2025-07-21 |title=Advanced version of Gemini with Deep Think officially achieves gold-medal standard at the International Mathematical Olympiad |url=https://deepmind.google/blog/advanced-version-of-gemini-with-deep-think-officially-achieves-gold-medal-standard-at-the-international-mathematical-olympiad/ |access-date=2026-08-24 |website=Google DeepMind |language=en}}</ref> However, mathematicians including [[Terence Tao]] and [[Kevin Buzzard]] cautioned that these claims were not based on reproducible experimental conditions and reflected neither a fair comparison to the human competitors nor the sort of performance that would be needed for research-level mathematics.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Riehl |first=Emily |author-link=Emily Riehl |date=August 7, 2025 |title=AI Took on the Math Olympiad—But Mathematicians Aren't Impressed |journal=[[Scientific American]] |volume=333 |issue=4 |page=59 |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican112025-22iPSyTcp1L7MIWqP5JvlJ |pmid=41085437 }}</ref> Journalists later revealed that the solutions submitted by OpenAI had not even been evaluated by the organization when the company announced its alleged "gold-medal level performance". Furthermore, when one of its solutions was evaluated it was deemed worthy of zero points because the chatbot “could guess the final result but not prove any part in a correct way”.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lis |first=Patricia Fernández de |date=2026-03-22 |title=Cómo los gigantes de la IA intentaron tomar al asalto el último reducto de la mente humana: las olimpiadas matemáticas |url=https://elpais.com/ciencia/2026-03-22/como-los-gigantes-de-la-ia-intentaron-tomar-al-asalto-el-ultimo-reducto-de-la-mente-humana-las-olimpiadas-matematicas.html |access-date=2026-08-24 |website=El País |language=es}}</ref>

===Penalties and bans===
North Korea is the only country to ever be disqualified for cheating, once at the 32nd IMO in 1991<ref>{{cite journal
 | author-last = Woodrow |author-first = Robert E.  | title = The Olympiad corner No.129 | year = 1991 | journal = [[Crux Mathematicorum]] | volume = 17 | issue = 9 | pages = 257 | url = https://smc.math.ca/wp-content/uploads/crux-pdfs/Crux_v17n09_Nov.pdf | access-date = 2023-09-24 }}</ref> and again at the 51st IMO in 2010.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imo-official.org/country_team_r.aspx?code=PRK|title=International Mathematical Olympiad: Democratic People's Republic of Korea|access-date=2010-07-17}}</ref> However, the incident in 2010 was controversial.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imo-register.org.uk/2010-report.html|title=International Mathematical Olympiad 2010 UK leader's report, Almaty and Astana, Kazakhstan|author=Geoff Smith |website = UK IMO Register |access-date=2023-09-06}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h357005|title=North Korea's disqualification at IMO 2010. |website=Art of Problem Solving|access-date=2023-09-06}}</ref> There have been other cases of cheating where contestants received penalties, although these cases were not officially disclosed. (For instance, at the 34th IMO in 1993, a contestant was disqualified for bringing a pocket book of formulas, and two contestants were awarded zero points on second day's paper for bringing calculators.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imo-register.org.uk/1993-report.html|title=34th International Mathematical Olympiad, Istanbul, Turkey, UK leader's report |author = Adam McBride |website = UK IMO Register |access-date=2023-11-24}}</ref>)

Russia has been banned from participating in the Olympiad since 2022 as a response to its [[Russian invasion of Ukraine|invasion of Ukraine]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2022-03-31 |title=International Mathematical Olympiad |url=https://www.imo-official.org/ |access-date=2023-12-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220331101006/https://www.imo-official.org/ |archive-date=31 March 2022 }}</ref> Nonetheless, a limited number of students (specifically, 6) are allowed to take part in the competition and receive awards, but only remotely and with their results being excluded from the unofficial team ranking. Slightly more than a half of the IMO 2021 Jury members (59 out of 107) voted in support of the sanction proposed by the IMO Board in an online voting in March 2022.<ref name=":1" />

In May 2025, a letter signed by over 700 mathematicians, amongst whom are [[Fields Medal]] recipients and a former Israeli IMO contestant, has called on the IMO Board to suspend the membership of Israel in the 2025 IMO for [[Gaza genocide|its war crimes in Gaza]] in the same way as the Board did to Russia. The letter cites as one of the reasons that the Palestinian IMO team members were blocked by the Israeli authorities from leaving the country for the 2024 IMO. The president of the IMO Board has refused to act, claiming that the Jury may decide during the 2025 IMO. The letter, however, accuses him of preventing the Jury from discussing the issue during the 2024 IMO by invoking a newly-added obscure regulation.<ref>{{cite news|url= https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/jun/07/the-longest-division-can-palestinian-and-israeli-students-compete-at-the-international-maths-olympiad|title= The longest division: can Palestinian and Israeli students compete at the International Maths Olympiad?| work= The Guardian|author= Joe Hinchliffe|date=6 June 2025|access-date=28 June 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Mathematics and Moral Responsibility: The IMO and the Genocide in Gaza| url=https://aurdip.org/en/mathematics-and-moral-responsibility-the-imo-and-the-genocide-in-gaza/|website= AURDIP| date = 18 May 2025 | access-date= 28 June 2025}}</ref>

===National achievements===
{{see also|List of countries by medal count at International Mathematical Olympiad}}
The following nations have achieved the highest team score in the respective competition:

* China, 26 times: in 1989, 1990, 1992, 1993, 1995, 1997, 1999 (joint), 2000–2002, 2004–2006, 2008–2011, 2013, 2014, 2019 (joint), 2020–2023, 2025-2026;<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=International Mathematical Olympiad – People's Republic of China – Team Results |url=https://www.imo-official.org/country_team_r.aspx?code=CHN |access-date=2026-07-20 |website=www.imo-official.org}}</ref>
* Russia (including [[Soviet Union]]), 16 times: in 1963–1967, 1972–1974, 1976, 1979, 1984, 1986 (joint), 1988, 1991, 1999 (joint), 2007;<ref name=rus/><ref name=ussr>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imo-official.org/country_team_r.aspx?code=USS|title=International Mathematical Olympiad – Union of Soviet Socialist Republics – Team Results|website=Imo-official.org|access-date=8 November 2021}}</ref>
* United States, 9 times: in 1977, 1981, 1986 (joint), 1994, 2015, 2016, 2018, 2019 (joint), 2024;<ref name=usa/>
* Hungary, 6 times: in 1961, 1962, 1969–1971, 1975;<ref name=hun>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imo-official.org/country_team_r.aspx?code=HUN|title=International Mathematical Olympiad – Hungary – Team Results|website=Imo-official.org|access-date=8 November 2021}}</ref>
* Romania, 5 times: in 1959, 1978, 1985, 1987, 1996;<ref name=rou>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imo-official.org/country_team_r.aspx?code=ROU|title=International Mathematical Olympiad – Romania – Team Results|website=Imo-official.org|access-date=8 November 2021}}</ref>
* West Germany, twice: in 1982 and 1983;<ref name=ger>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imo-official.org/country_team_r.aspx?code=GER|title=International Mathematical Olympiad – Germany – Team Results|website=Imo-official.org|access-date=8 November 2021}}</ref>
* South Korea, twice: in 2012 and 2017;<ref name=rok/>
* Bulgaria, once: in 2003;<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mmjp.or.jp/jmo/imo2003/contents/results_all.txt|title=Results of the 44th International Mathematical Olympiad|website=Mmjp.or.jp|access-date=2008-03-05|archive-date=2 May 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080502185609/http://www.mmjp.or.jp/jmo/imo2003/contents/results_all.txt|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* Iran, once: in 1998;<ref name=irn>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imo-official.org/country_team_r.aspx?code=GDR|title=International Mathematical Olympiad – Islamic Republic of Iran – Team Results|website=Imo-official.org|access-date=8 November 2021}}</ref>
* East Germany, once: in 1968.<ref name=gdr>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imo-official.org/country_team_r.aspx?code=GDR|title=International Mathematical Olympiad – German Democratic Republic – Team Results|website=Imo-official.org|access-date=8 November 2021}}</ref>

The following nations have achieved an all-members-gold IMO with a full team:

* China, 16 times: in 1992, 1993, 1997, 2000–2002, 2004, 2006, 2009–2011, 2019, 2021–2023, 2025.<ref name=":0" />
* United States, 4 times: in 1994, 2011, 2016, and 2019.<ref name=usa>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imo-official.org/country_team_r.aspx?code=USA|title=International Mathematical Olympiad – United States of America – Team Results|website=Imo-official.org|access-date=8 November 2021}}</ref>
* South Korea, 3 times: in 2012, 2017, and 2019.<ref name=rok>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imo-official.org/country_team_r.aspx?code=KOR|title=International Mathematical Olympiad – Republic of Korea – Team Results|website=Imo-official.org|access-date=8 November 2021}}</ref>
* Russia, twice: in 2002 and 2008.<ref name=rus>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imo-official.org/country_team_r.aspx?code=RUS|title=International Mathematical Olympiad – Russian Federation – Team Results|website=Imo-official.org|access-date=8 November 2021}}</ref>
* Bulgaria, once: in 2003.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imo-official.org/country_team_r.aspx?code=BGR|title=International Mathematical Olympiad – Bulgaria – Team Results|website=Imo-official.org|access-date=8 November 2021}}</ref>

The only countries to have their entire team score perfectly in the IMO were the United States in 1994, China in 2022, and Luxembourg, whose 1-member team had a perfect score in 1981. The US's success earned a mention in ''[[TIME Magazine]]''.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,981185,00.html|title=No. 1 and Counting|access-date=2010-02-23 | magazine=Time | date=1994-08-01}}</ref> Hungary won IMO 1975 in an unorthodox way when none of the eight team members received a gold medal (five silver, three bronze).<ref name=hun/> The second-place team, East Germany, also did not have a single gold medal winner (four silver, four bronze).<ref name=gdr/>

The current ten countries with the best all-time results are as follows:<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imo-official.org/results_country.aspx?column=awards&order=asc|title=Results: Cumulative Results by Country|website=Imo-official.org|access-date=2023-07-29}}</ref>

===Individual achievements===
{{see also|List of International Mathematical Olympiad participants}}
[[File:Zhuo Qun (Alex) Song.jpg|thumb|[[Zhuo Qun Song]] at the 2015 IMO]]
Several participants have achieved notable success at the International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO): [[Alex Chui]] (United Kingdom) is the most decorated IMO participant in history,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Murning |first=Vix |date=2026-07-21 |title=British Pupil Wins International Maths Olympiad, Becomes Most Decorated Participant of All Time |url=https://ukmt.org.uk/british-pupil-wins-international-maths-olympiad |access-date=2026-07-25 |website=[[United Kingdom Mathematics Trust|UKMT]] |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Nga|first=Minh|date=2026-07-22|title=Teen boy secures historic 5th International Math Olympiad gold with perfect score - VnExpress International|url=https://e.vnexpress.net/news/news/education/teen-boy-secures-historic-5th-international-math-olympiad-gold-with-perfect-score-5100733.html|archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20260724042833/https://e.vnexpress.net/news/news/education/teen-boy-secures-historic-5th-international-math-olympiad-gold-with-perfect-score-5100733.html|archive-date=2026-07-24|access-date=2026-07-25|work=[[VnExpress]] International|language=en}}</ref> having won five gold medals (including a perfect score in 2026) and two silver medals.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Hall of Fame - International Mathematical Olympiad |url=https://www.imo-official.org/hall-of-fame/ |url-status=live |access-date=2026-07-20 |website=International Mathematical Olympiad Official}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Individual Results-IMO 2026 |url=https://www.imo2026.com/Results/Individual_Results.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260719174632/https://www.imo2026.com/Results/Individual_Results.htm |archive-date=2026-07-19 |access-date=2026-07-20 |website=www.imo2026.com}}</ref> Prior to 2026, Zhuo Qun Song (Canada) previously held the record for most gold medals, with five golds and one bronze (including a perfect score in 2015).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imo-official.org/hall.aspx |title=International Mathematical Olympiad Hall of Fame |publisher=Imo-official.org |access-date=2015-07-15|website=International Mathematical Olympiad|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260516125446/https://www.imo-official.org/hall-of-fame/|archive-date=2026-05-16|url-status=deviated}}</ref> [[Reid W. Barton|Reid Barton]] (United States) was the first participant to win four gold medals (1998–2001).<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://www.sciencemag.org/cgi/content/summary/293/5530/597|title=IMO's Golden Boy Makes Perfection Look Easy|access-date=2008-03-05 | doi=10.1126/science.293.5530.597|pmid=11474084|volume=293|issue=5530|journal=Science|page=597|year=2001|last1=MacKenzie|first1=D.|s2cid=8587484|url-access=subscription}}</ref> He is also one of ten four-time [[William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition#Putnam Fellows|Putnam Fellow]]s (2001–04). Seven participants in total have achieved four gold medals. Aside from Barton, these include: [[Christian Reiher]] (Germany): 2000–03 (also earned a bronze medal in 1999), [[Lisa Sauermann]] (Germany): 2008–11 (also earned a silver medal in 2007), {{ill|Teodor von Burg|sr|Теодор фон Бург}} (Serbia): 2009–12 (also earned a silver in 2008 and a bronze in 2007), Nipun Pitimanaaree (Thailand): 2011–14 (also earned a silver medal in 2009), Luke Robitaille (United States): 2019–22, and Alexander Wang (United States): 2023–26.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imo-official.org/hall.aspx|title=International Mathematical Olympiad Hall of Fame|access-date=2009-07-18}}</ref> Barton, Robitaille, and Wang are the only contestants to have won four gold medals without receiving any other medal color.<ref name=":2" /> Wolfgang Burmeister (East Germany), Martin Härterich (West Germany), Iurie Boreico (Moldova), and Lim Jeck (Singapore) are the only other participants besides Reiher, Sauermann, von Burg, and Pitimanaaree to win five medals with at least three of them gold.<ref name="more">{{cite web|url=https://www.imo-register.org.uk/2017-report.pdf|title=Geoff Smith (August 2017). "UK IMO team leader's report". University of Bath. |access-date=2018-07-02}}</ref> [[Ciprian Manolescu]] (Romania) managed to write a perfect paper (42 points) for gold medal more times than anybody else in the history of the competition, doing it all three times he participated in the IMO (1995, 1996, 1997).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.unl.edu/amc/e-exams/e9-imo/imoteamrecord.shtml|title=IMO team record|access-date=2008-03-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080220172111/http://www.unl.edu/amc/e-exams/e9-imo/imoteamrecord.shtml|archive-date=2008-02-20|url-status=dead}}</ref> Manolescu is also a three-time Putnam Fellow (1997, 1998, 2000).<ref name="putnam">{{cite web|url=http://www.maa.org/awards/putnam.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000229230334/http://www.maa.org/awards/putnam.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=2000-02-29|title=The Mathematical Association of America's William Lowell Putnam Competition|access-date=2008-03-05}}</ref> [[Eugenia Malinnikova]] ([[Soviet Union]]) is the highest-scoring female contestant in IMO history. She has 3 gold medals in IMO 1989 (41 points), IMO 1990 (42) and IMO 1991 (42), missing only 1 point in 1989 to precede Manolescu's achievement.<ref>{{Cite book
 |last=Vakil
 |first=Ravi
 |author-link=Ravi Vakil
 |title=A Mathematical Mosaic: Patterns & Problem Solving
 |publisher=Brendan Kelly Publishing
 |year=1997
 |isbn=978-1-895997-28-6
 |page=288
 }}</ref>

[[Terence Tao]] (Australia) participated in IMO 1986, 1987 and 1988, winning bronze, silver and gold medals respectively. He won a gold medal when he just turned thirteen in IMO 1988, becoming the youngest person<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iht.com/articles/2007/03/13/news/math.php|title=A packed house for a math lecture? Must be Terence Tao|website=Iht.com|access-date=2008-03-05}}</ref> to receive a gold medal (Zhuo Qun Song of Canada also won a gold medal at age 13, in 2011, though he was older than Tao). Tao also holds the distinction of being the youngest medalist with his 1986 bronze medal, followed by 2009 bronze medalist [[Raúl Chávez Sarmiento]] (Peru), at the age of 10 and 11 respectively.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.livinginperu.com/news/9641 |title=Peru won four silver and two bronze medals in International Math Olympiad |date=July 22, 2009 |website=Livinginperu.com }}</ref>

===Gender gap and the launch of European Girls' Mathematical Olympiad===
Over the years, since its inception to present, the IMO has attracted far more male contestants than female contestants.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Whitney|first=A. K.|date=2016-04-18|title=Why Does the Gender Gap Persist in International Math Competitions?|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/education/archive/2016/04/girls-math-international-competiton/478533/|access-date=2021-08-15|website=The Atlantic|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Loewus|first=Liana|date=2015-07-27|title=Gender Gaps at the Math Olympiad: Where Are the Girls?|url=https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/gender-gaps-at-the-math-olympiad-where-are-the-girls/2015/07|access-date=2021-08-15|website=Education Week|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.ft.com/content/8d9dba28-ae17-11e9-b3e2-4fdf846f48f5 |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20221210/https://www.ft.com/content/8d9dba28-ae17-11e9-b3e2-4fdf846f48f5 |archive-date=10 December 2022 |url-access=subscription|title=The biggest gender divide is in mathematics|newspaper=[[Financial Times]]|date=5 September 2019|last1=Hoyos|first1=Carola}}</ref> During the period 2000–2021, there were only 1,102 female contestants (9.2%) out of a total of 11,950 contestants. The gap is even more significant in terms of IMO gold medallists; from 1959 to 2021, there were 43 female (3.3%) and 1295 male gold medal winners.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imo-official.org/hall.aspx?column=awards&order=desc&gender=filter&block=1&nameform=western|title = International Mathematical Olympiad|website=Imo-official.org}}</ref>

This gender gap in participation and in performance at the IMO level led to the establishment of the [[European Girls' Mathematical Olympiad]] (EGMO).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2015/oct/13/mathematical-ratios-competition-girls-plus-or-minus|title=Mathematical ratios: Is a competition just for girls a plus or a minus?|website=[[TheGuardian.com]]|date=13 October 2015}}</ref>

==Media coverage==
* A documentary, "Hard Problems: The Road To The World's Toughest Math Contest" was made about the United States 2006 IMO team.<ref>[http://www.hardproblemsmovie.com/ ''Hard Problems: The Road to the World's Toughest Math Contest''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100715212537/http://www.hardproblemsmovie.com/ |date=2010-07-15 }}, Zala Films and the [[Mathematical Association of America]], 2008.</ref>
* A BBC documentary titled ''[[Beautiful Young Minds]]'' aired July 2007 about the performance of British prodigy [[Daniel Lightwing]] taking part in the IMO and struggling with [[Asperger's syndrome]]. It inspired the BBC film ''[[X+Y]]'' (2014), a fictionalized version of Lightwing's story.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.yorkpress.co.uk/leisure/film/11868140.Meet_the_York_College_student_who_inspired_the_film_X_Y/|title=Meet the York College student who inspired the film X+Y|last=Hutchinson|first=Charles|date=19 March 2015|newspaper=[[The Press (York)]]|access-date=2025-12-30}}</ref>
* A book named ''Countdown'' by Steve Olson tells the story of the United States team's success in the 2001 Olympiad.<ref name=olson>{{Cite book|last=Olson|first=Steve|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-ctkwbaws7gC|title=Count Down: Six Kids Vie for Glory at the World's Toughest Math Competition|date=2005|publisher=Houghton Mifflin Harcourt|isbn=978-0-618-56212-1|language=en}}</ref>
